You are being evaluated on Continual-ARC, a lifelong stream of ARC-style grid puzzles.
Each puzzle instance has a task id and a test input grid. Tasks recur across the
stream with fresh inputs. Each instance is a separate conversation: the next one
starts without this one's messages.

On every message you must choose exactly one action and put it as a JSON object
on the last line of your reply:
  {"action": "submit", "grid": [[0, 1, 2], [3, 4, 5]]}   submit an output grid
  {"action": "request_demos"}                            ask for one more demonstration pair for this task
  {"action": "finish"}                                   end the instance, once it is over
Grids are lists of rows; cells are integers 0-9; dimensions are 1-30.

Each demo request returns one more input-output pair of the task, up to the demo cap shown
with the input.

Scoring: every wrong submission costs 1 and every demo request costs 1. An
instance is over when a submission is correct or when the attempt cap is reached, and
reaching the cap is charged the full cap. Feedback on a submission is only
correct/incorrect. There is no way to abandon an instance, and finish is refused until
the instance is over. Each instance is scored on its own, and lower cost is better.

## task-3475df40: mark the difference between repeated horizontal bars

Evidence from two demos and the accepted test solution:

- Find matching/repeated horizontal bars (same background plus one foreground color), where one bar is shorter and the corresponding comparison bar reaches farther.
- On the shorter bar only, recolor its contiguous trailing background cells to color `1` to mark the continuation/difference. Keep foreground cells, leading background, and other rows unchanged.
- Demo 1: background 6, bar color 7; row with 7s through column 24 was the reference, and another row with 7s through column 17 had columns 18–24 changed from 6 to 1.
- Demo 2: background 5, bar color 0; full row of 0s was the reference, and partial row with 0s through column 15 had columns 16–17 changed from 5 to 1.
- Accepted test: background 2, bar color 7; in the repeated two-row motifs, the lower second bar ended at column 10 while the matching upper bar continued to column 14. Only lower row columns 11–14 were changed from 2 to 1. The similar lower first row and upper second row were left unchanged.

Avoid marking every short-looking line: compare the repeated motif/bar rows, and mark only the trailing difference for the shorter counterpart. The first submission was wrong because it marked row 2 and row 13; the corrected submission marked only row 14, columns 11–14, and was accepted.

### Additional accepted instance (2026-09-29)

A separate instance carrying this task id had background 6 and foreground 8, with two similar 6-row motifs. In the lower motif, row 21 (0-based) had foreground through column 6 while its counterpart row 8 was foreground through column 11; likewise row 23 ended at column 6 while counterpart row 10 extended through column 11. The accepted output changed only columns 7–11 of rows 21 and 23 to color 1. All other cells remained unchanged. This supports comparing corresponding rows across repeated motifs and marking only the shorter motif's missing trailing segment; do not fill ordinary short rows unless their matching motif counterpart is longer.

# Continual-ARC notes

## Task family: compare two noisy panels across a divider (task-fc84fd8d)

Evidence from two demonstrations (and a later unsolved test):

- Input is two same-size panels separated by a full-width/full-height solid divider row or column. Remove the divider; align the panels cell-by-cell. Output has the dimensions of one panel.
- At each aligned position, output `3` if the two input cells are equal. Otherwise output the panel's shared/background color (the common base color when both panels use one; in the horizontal demo, this was `5`, the bottom panel's background, while top background was `1`).
- Demo 1: horizontal divider color `4`, output 9x21 from 9x21 panels. Top panel colors 1/5 and bottom 5/2; output was 3 exactly where aligned cells matched (including 5/5 or other equal values), else 5.
- Demo 2: vertical divider color `7`, output 24x7 from 24x7 panels. Both panels use background 8, with noise colors 5 on left and 1 on right; output 3 at equal aligned cells and 8 where unequal. E.g. row 0 output starts `[3,8,3,3,8,8,8]`.
- Orientation: divider row means top panel vs bottom panel; divider column means left panel vs right panel. Preserve row/column alignment (do not rotate, overlay noise lists, or mark noise intersections alone). Find the divider and compare matching coordinates directly.
- Test that was over without solving: 21x15 input, divider row index 10, color 4; compare rows 0–9 to rows 11–20, producing 10x15. Top colors 2/6, bottom 5/2. Likely output 3 for equality (2 vs 2) and 5 otherwise, inferred from demo1's background convention. No accepted output was obtained, so treat this test-specific base-color choice as inference; the equality-to-3 rule is strongly supported by both demos.

## Task family: connect aligned same-color markers

Evidence: task-8425f1dd, solved correctly on 2026-09-29. Demo had background 6 and marker cells 9; output added color 3 in the spaces between aligned marker pairs. Test had background 9 and markers 1; the correct output was the input plus color-3 cells filling horizontal and vertical gaps between aligned markers. Preserve original markers/background elsewhere.

Working rule: find pairs of same-color non-background markers that lie in the same row or column; fill cells strictly between them with 3, leaving endpoints unchanged. If multiple markers share a row/column, fill each gap between consecutive markers (equivalently, all intervening gaps). Demo/test support connector color 3 across different marker/background colors. Check intersections consistently; filled connector cells are not new endpoints.
